strengths: Addresses an important limitation of human animation: binding distinct audio streams to the correct people while preserving multiple reference appearances.
The supervised mask predictor and reuse of masks across denoising steps provide a plausible, practical mechanism for spatial audio conditioning without user-supplied layouts.

Reported results are promising: compared with fixed-mask conditioning, Sync-D improves from 7.068 to 6.670 and FVD from 40.239 to 22.881. Table 3 also shows consistent improvements in reference-image and facial fidelity over the evaluated baselines.
The paper includes several conditioning baselines, human preference evaluations, and useful supplementary descriptions of training and data processing.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately establish the central claim of correct identity–audio binding. Quantitative multi-person tests contain only two people, with one speaking and one silent; the identity-specific Sync-D computation and listener leakage assessment are unspecified. More seriously, Appendix E explicitly tells human evaluators that it does not matter who is speaking, so this study cannot validate assignment to the intended identity. Alternating speakers, simultaneous independent speech, and identity swaps need direct evaluation.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed iterative mechanism. There are no mask accuracy measurements, refinement curves, comparisons with same-step prediction or ground-truth dynamic masks, or sensitivity analyses for the ten-step warm-up and layer aggregation. Appendix B identifies the global and fixed-mask variants as the pretrained audio model, leaving additional multi-concept training and mask supervision confounded with the conditioning mechanism.

Algorithm 1 contradicts the core method description: it overwrites the previous-mask cache before audio injection and uses current masks rather than cached previous-step masks. It also places audio injection outside the DiT-layer loop, whereas the text describes per-block injection, and averages all layers rather than the last few. These discrepancies obscure how the principal contribution is actually implemented.

Experimental reliability and comparison fairness are insufficiently documented. The audio test-set sizes, identity-disjoint splits, uncertainty estimates, and detailed FVD protocol are not reported. The human study uses only 19 and 9 examples with ten raters and provides no uncertainty or randomization details. Comparisons involve different backbones, training resources, and input requirements without enough controls to attribute gains to the proposed architecture.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the supplementary training settings. The work relies on an internal 2.6-million-example corpus and a pretrained audio-driven foundation whose exact checkpoint, model scale, and full training configuration are not specified. Output resolution, video length, inference cost, and quantitative overhead are also missing, leaving the claimed efficiency unsupported.

Several broader claims exceed the evidence. Long-video generation, robust human–object interaction, and scaling to more identities lack dedicated evaluations. The technical novelty is principally an integration of reference-token attention, supervised segmentation, and masked audio attention; without stronger controlled evidence for iterative mask reuse, the contribution is not yet sufficiently established for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: binding separate audio streams to the correct people in multi-concept video generation without requiring user-provided layouts.
Predicting reference-conditioned masks and reusing them across denoising steps is a plausible, practical extension of an audio-conditioned video diffusion model.

Reported results are promising: multi-person Sync-D improves from 7.068 with fixed masks to 6.670, and FVD improves from 40.239 to 22.881. Table 3 also shows consistent gains in appearance fidelity over the evaluated baselines.
The paper includes alternative conditioning baselines, qualitative examples, user preferences, and supplementary training details.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately establish the central claim of identity-specific audio control. Quantitative multi-person testing uses only one speaker and one muted listener. Appendix E.1 explicitly tells participants that the identity of the speaker does not matter, so the user study cannot validate correct audio-to-identity assignment. Alternating dialogue, simultaneous speakers, and identity swaps need direct evaluation.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate the proposed contribution. Appendix B identifies global audio as the pretrained OmniHuman model and fixed masks as an inference modification of that model, whereas the proposed system receives additional multi-concept training. Improvements can therefore reflect training differences. Matched-training comparisons, mask-supervision ablations, and comparisons of cached versus same-step masks are missing.

The implementation description is inconsistent at the core of the method. Section 3.3 and Figure 2 use previous-step masks for audio attention within DiT blocks, but Algorithm 1 overwrites the cache before audio injection, uses current masks, and places audio injection outside the block loop. It also averages all layers rather than the last few specified in the text. These discrepancies obstruct faithful reproduction.

Evidence for reliable layout prediction is insufficient. There are no quantitative mask-accuracy results, refinement curves across denoising steps, or controlled tests of occlusion and crossing subjects. The claims of progressive improvement and robust alignment are asserted rather than demonstrated, and the ten-step warm-up is not ablated.

Evaluation reporting limits confidence in the gains. Audio benchmark sizes, identity-disjoint train/test separation, multi-person face-to-audio matching procedures, and uncertainty estimates are unspecified. The user study involves only ten participants and 19 audio examples or nine customization examples, without confidence intervals or sufficient sampling and randomization details.

Reproducibility and comparative attribution remain limited by the internal training corpus, insufficiently specified base-model scale/checkpoint, and absent runtime or memory measurements. Comparisons against commercial systems and the 1.3B Phantom variant do not establish how much improvement comes from the proposed mechanism versus backbone and data differences.

Claims about long-video generation, broad human-object interactions, and scaling to arbitrary numbers of concepts extend beyond the demonstrated evaluation. Overall, the practical idea and positive results are outweighed by unresolved validation and reproducibility issues at a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful problem: binding separate audio signals to the correct people in video generation conditioned on multiple reference images.
The combination of reference-conditioned mask prediction and cached masks for spatial audio injection is intuitive and practically motivated.

Reported results are promising: predicted masks improve multi-person Sync-D from 7.068 to 6.670 and FVD from 40.239 to 22.881 relative to fixed masks. Concept-fidelity metrics and user preferences also favor the method.
Provides implementation details, alternative conditioning baselines, and a substantial automated data-curation pipeline.
weaknesses: The central identity-binding claim is inadequately evaluated. Appendix E explicitly tells raters that it does not matter who is speaking, so the user study cannot establish correct audio-to-identity assignment. The automatic evaluation does not clearly specify identity matching or measure unintended listener speech.

Quantitative audio evaluation is restricted to two people with one speaker. It does not substantiate broader claims about alternating dialogue, multiple simultaneous audio streams, more participants, or long-video generation.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed iterative mechanism. There are no mask-accuracy measurements, refinement curves, cache or warm-up ablations, or comparisons against ground-truth dynamic masks. Algorithm 1 contradicts the central description: it overwrites the mask cache before audio injection and uses current masks rather than previous-step masks. Evaluation reproducibility is limited: the collected two-person test-set size, train/test separation, identity-association procedure, and statistical uncertainty are not reported. The user study includes only ten raters and 19/9 examples, while comparisons involve commercial systems and a small public Phantom model without controlled backbone or training budgets.

The private training corpus and incompletely specified base model constrain independent verification. The promising application and reported gains do not yet outweigh the gaps in validating the paper's central contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of audio-driven animation: binding distinct audio tracks to the correct identities while allowing people to move and interact. Supporting separate reference images without requiring a composed first frame is practically useful.

The proposed combination of supervised per-identity mask prediction and spatially gated audio attention is plausible and relatively lightweight. The reported predictor adds 56M parameters to a 7B backbone, with measured runtime overhead.

Reported results are encouraging: on the multi-person benchmark, the method improves Sync-D to 6.670 and FVD to 22.881, compared with 7.671 and 35.472 for MultiTalk. The customization benchmark also shows improvements in identity fidelity and visual quality.

The appendix provides useful additional evidence, including mask IoU across denoising steps, a cache ablation, single-person benchmarks, and preliminary results with four to five subjects. The paper also acknowledges mask failures under occlusion.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately establish the central claim of correct identity-specific audio assignment. Appendix F.1 explicitly tells human raters that 'it doesn’t matter specifically who is speaking,' allowing a method that animates the wrong identity to score well. The objective evaluation does not clearly specify how generated faces are matched to the intended speaker or separately measure unintended listener speech.

The primary multi-person benchmark assumes two participants with only one speaking. This is substantially narrower than the claimed multi-person dialogue capability. There is no convincing quantitative evaluation of turn-taking, simultaneous distinct audio tracks, or identity preservation through crossings and occlusions. Table 13 adds four-to-five-person results but omits sample counts and the speaking protocol.

The main ablations do not cleanly isolate the proposed mechanism. Appendix C.4 states that global audio uses the pretrained model and fixed masks are applied to that pretrained model, whereas the proposed system receives multi-concept training. Consequently, Table 4 can conflate dynamic masking with additional training. A matched-training comparison and an oracle dynamic-mask upper bound would make the causal evidence substantially stronger.

Benchmark reporting is insufficient for assessing reliability. The sizes and construction details of the main audio test sets, train/test identity separation, FVD sampling protocol, and uncertainty estimates are missing. The user study involves only ten raters and 19 audio examples or nine customization examples, without confidence intervals. The mask-IoU analysis also does not clearly establish how ground-truth masks are obtained and aligned with generated trajectories.

The inference pseudocode contradicts the central description. Algorithm 1 overwrites the cache before audio injection and gates with the current mask rather than the previous-step mask. It also places audio injection outside the DiT-layer loop and averages all layers, whereas the text describes per-block injection and aggregation over the last few blocks. These discrepancies materially obstruct reproduction of the claimed cache mechanism.

Novelty and comparative positioning need stronger support. Ingredients already predicts identity layouts, while MultiTalk and HunyuanVideo-Avatar support multi-person audio animation. The potentially distinctive contribution is their integration with reference-conditioned dynamic audio routing, but the paper does not adequately isolate this advance experimentally. HunyuanVideo-Avatar receives only a capability comparison, and the advertised Wan2.1 reimplementation has no reported results establishing that it reproduces the main model's gains.

Table 13 provides four-to-five-person scores without sufficient dataset or protocol details to establish robust scaling.

The main ablations do not cleanly isolate the proposed mechanism. Appendix C.4 identifies global-audio and fixed-mask variants as the pretrained OmniHuman model, whereas the proposed method receives additional multi-concept training. Consequently, Table 4 cannot separate architectural gains from training gains. A matched-training comparison and a ground-truth dynamic-mask upper bound would strengthen the evidence.

Algorithm 1 contradicts the central previous-step caching description: it overwrites the cache before audio injection and uses current masks rather than the previous cached masks. It also places audio injection outside the DiT-layer loop, unlike the architecture description. These discrepancies affect reproducibility of the main contribution, rather than merely notation.

Experimental reporting is insufficient for judging reliability. The main multi-person test-set size, train/test identity separation, uncertainty estimates, and detailed baseline input protocols are not established. The human study uses only 19 audio examples and nine customization examples with ten raters. The reported Wan2.1 reimplementation does not itself establish reproducibility of results obtained with the main 7B backbone.

Novelty and positioning require sharper qualification. Ingredients already predicts identity layouts, and the paper acknowledges concurrent multi-person audio systems. The distinctive contribution is their integration with iterative local audio conditioning, but broad first-method claims exceed that distinction. HunyuanVideo-Avatar receives only a capability comparison, and customization comparisons against the 1.3B Phantom variant leave model-capacity effects unresolved.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: generating multi-person animation from separate reference images while binding each audio track to the appropriate person. Combining reference-conditioned layout prediction with localized audio injection is a sensible design.

Reported quantitative results are promising. On the multi-person benchmark, the method improves Sync-D over MultiTalk (6.670 versus 7.671) and fixed-mask OmniHuman (7.068), while achieving substantially lower FVD (22.881 versus 35.472 and 40.239).

The evaluation covers appearance preservation, single-person animation, user preferences, computational overhead, and several conditioning ablations. Appendix experiments additionally examine mask refinement, caching, and generation with four to five people.

The paper acknowledges meaningful limitations, including overlapping identities, coarse mask boundaries, and reduced prompt diversity. The mask predictor adds relatively few parameters to the backbone.
weaknesses: The central claim of correct identity-to-audio binding is insufficiently evaluated. The main benchmark contains two people with only one speaking, and the Sync-D protocol does not explain how the evaluated face is matched to the intended reference identity or how unintended listener speech is penalized. More seriously, Appendix F explicitly tells human raters that it does not matter who is speaking. This study therefore cannot establish the claimed identity-specific control.

Important evaluation details are missing: the size and construction of the main two-person test set, separation from training identities/videos, sample counts for mask-IoU and four-to-five-person experiments, and uncertainty estimates. The user study includes only 10 raters and 19 audio-driven examples or 9 customization examples. Table 13 alone, without a defined protocol, provides limited support for scaling to additional speakers or realistic dialogue.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate the proposed mechanism. Appendix C.4 identifies global-audio and fixed-mask variants as extensions of the pretrained audio model, whereas the proposed model receives additional multi-concept training and mask supervision. Consequently, differences in FVD and synchronization may reflect training differences as well as dynamic masking. Matched-training controls and a genuine per-frame oracle-mask comparison would strengthen attribution.

Algorithm 1 contradicts the defining cross-timestep caching mechanism. It computes current masks, overwrites the cache before audio injection, and gates audio with the current masks; the previous-mask variable is never read. It also places audio injection outside the DiT-block loop, unlike the description in Section 3.2. These are material ambiguities in reproducing the core method, even if they are pseudocode errors rather than implementation flaws.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful architectural and optimization details. The reported results use a 7B backbone with substantial audio pretraining and a largely unavailable curated dataset, while the reproducibility statement describes a Wan2.1 reimplementation without reporting its performance. This leaves unclear whether the accessible implementation reproduces the demonstrated gains.

The contribution is promising, but its distinction from existing layout-prediction customization methods and concurrent multi-person talking systems needs stronger controlled evidence. Taken together, the identity-control evaluation gap, confounded ablations, and inconsistent algorithm description prevent the current submission from meeting the acceptance threshold.
